name: Removing Names Before Data Goes In
title: Removing Names Before Data Goes In
answer: Removing names before data goes into an AI tool is the simplest and most effective privacy habit for schools. It means stripping out names, student ID numbers, birth dates, addresses, and school names, plus any detail that could identify a child indirectly. It matters because it removes the most common privacy mistake with AI while still letting teachers get useful help.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: This idea is about taking identifying details out of student information before it is entered into any AI tool. The details to remove include names, student ID numbers, birth dates, addresses, and school names, and often more than that. Even without a name, a rare disability, a small grade level, or a specific family situation can point to a particular child. The problem it solves is the everyday privacy slip that happens when a teacher pastes full student information into a tool to get help thinking through a task. By removing the identifying layer first, the teacher can still use the tool while nothing in the exchange points to a real child.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, the habit works like this: before any student information goes into a tool, the teacher takes out the identifying details. The book gives a worked example in Figure 3.6, where a special education teacher wants help drafting a goal for a student's individualized education program. The version on the left includes everything the teacher knows, and the version on the right includes only what the tool needs to draft a goal. The draft that comes back is just as useful, and nothing in it points to a real child. The text does not give separate grade band examples, so the practice applies the same way across grade levels.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not present a study, figure, or formal finding for this idea beyond the worked example in Figure 3.6. That example shows a special education teacher drafting an individualized education program goal, with the full-information version on the left and the minimal-information version on the right, and the draft that comes back is just as useful while nothing in it points to a real child. The book's claim that removing names makes the most common privacy mistake with AI mostly disappear is presented as practice-based reasoning rather than research evidence. So this idea rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Removing names does not replace an approved tool or a signed agreement. It is a second layer of protection for the moments when a teacher uses AI to think through a problem, not a substitute for the formal approvals a school already requires. The decisions about which tools are approved and which agreements are signed stay with the school, not with the individual teacher. The text also notes that removing names is a habit worth building across the whole staff, which means the responsibility is shared rather than left to one person. When removing names becomes automatic, the most common privacy mistake with AI mostly disappears.
